Our view is that the battlefield of the 2030s has already been pulled forward by conflicts across Eurasia, from the Russia-Ukraine war to the US-Iran conflict. It was only a matter of time before Ukrainian forces paired heavy UAVs with unmanned ground vehicles to conduct offensive missions deep inside no-man's-land , where the majority of deaths are caused by kamikaze drones. Swamping human soldiers with robotics has been the evolution of warfare. With FPVs now responsible for the majority of battlefield casualties, combining aerial and ground robotic systems will become the new normal. X user Drone Wars published a new video that shows a Ukrainian UAV airlifting a UGV deep into the front lines. Footage reportedly shows a Ukrainian heavy UAV carrying a small unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) suspended beneath it. pic.twitter.com/IBDxbGtrFy — Drone Wars (@Drone_Wars_) July 18, 2026 A separate account, Counter Unmanned Systems , showcased the possible UGV featured in the video above. "Meet GNOM from Polish firm Macro-System ( @macro_system_ms ). With speed up to 80 km/h and weighing 7 kg with warhead is a light weight attritable system that has been part of various European armed force exercises," Counter Unmanned Systems wrote in the X post. Ground Loitering Munition 🇵🇱Meet GNOM from Polish firm Macro-System ( @macro_system_ms ). With speed up to 80 km/h and weighing 7 kg with warhead is a light weight attritable system that has been part of various European armed force exercises. More on GNOM >>… pic.twitter.com/dchzZrnFiO — Counter Unmanned Systems (@CUAS_NEWS) July 18, 2026 The combination of aerial drones and ground robots working together was inevitable. The deeper national security threat is the democratization of this technology. Drones, once restricted to militaries, can now be assembled and produced using commercially available parts, 3D printers, and components sourced through Chinese supply chains. Drones spreading to the Americas: Fiber-Optic Kamikaze Drone Found In Mexico Signals New Drone Threat South Of Border Easy to purchase, even on Facebook: Why Is China Advertising Insane War Drones On Facebook Those low barriers to entry will only ensure that these drones spread far beyond Eurasia's war zones and into the hands of proxy forces, insurgent groups and terrorist networks worldwide. The battlefield of the 2030s is already being built from commercially available parts. The world is becoming a dark and dangerous place as robots become weaponized. Humanoids will be next . Share it with your friends! Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn Romania is expected to promulgate four out of the six laws supposed to unlock EUR 5 billion of grants under the European Union’s Resilience Facility (RRF), after the Senate failed to endorse the Integrity Law on July 30, according to ProTV . The four laws, having received final green light from Parliament, two in the Chamber of Deputies and two in the Senate, unlock EUR 3.5 billion of grants, if assessed positively by the European Commission. Two last-minute amendments filed in the Senate by the Social Democrats (PSD) to the Integrity Law, approved by the Chamber of Deputies on the day before, prompted negative votes from Save Romania Union (USR) and the Liberal Party (PNL) – which plan to resume the legislation procedure next week. The amendments were specifically aimed at retroactively stripping USR president Dominic Fritz of its mayoral seat in Timisoara. The Integrity Law has a EUR 770 million grant attached, just like the Wage Law for the budgetary sector – the sixth law that was not yet filed for a vote in parliament due to massive protests of the trade unions and a lack of consensus among political parties. The four reforms passed by the Parliament should bring EUR 3.5 billion in grants, if promulgated by the end of August. Urban Planning Code / Senate The first reform, worth EUR 972 million under PNRR, the Urban Planning Code attempts to bring together in a single normative act the rules regarding territorial planning and construction authorisation. The project should merge provisions from the current legislation, simplify procedures and introduce more digitalisation. It was approved by the Senate and will be sent to the President for promulgation. For Bucharest, one of the most disputed provisions concerns building permits. The referendum held among Bucharest residents during the 2024 local elections provided for the transfer of this competence from the district mayors to the City Hall of the Capital. The bill has been in Parliament since 2023 and was tacitly adopted by the Senate. After several years of deadlock, this week's vote should determine the final shape of one of the most far-reaching reforms in construction. Decarbonising heating / Senate The second reform, worth EUR 972 million, concerns the decarbonization of the heating and cooling sector. The project aims to shift to heat pumps, solar energy, geothermal sources and other low-emission technologies. It also foresees a gradual reduction in the use of forest biomass and wood for heating. The first version of the bill was rejected by the Senate at the end of June, after not gathering enough votes. The reform was resumed, and PSD and UDMR submitted amendments. The vote has direct effects on investments in district heating and the modernisation of heating systems. It was approved by the Senate and will be sent to the President for promulgation. Bonuses for ANAF and Customs employees / Chamber of Deputies A third project introduces a system of rewarding employees of ANAF and the Customs Authority. Bonuses will depend on additional revenues brought to the budget and measurable performance indicators. The reform is associated with EUR 770 million in grants under the PNRR. The reward would be variable and temporary. The amounts awarded in a year cannot exceed 12% of the budget for basic salaries. For cases that bring the state over one million euros, the project provides for a separate reward, after the actual collection of the money and the final confirmation of the claim. The authors of the project claim that the system avoids turning bonuses into a permanent salary right. From a political point of view, the project has caused less tension. The Senate was the first chamber to be notified, and the final vote belonged to the Chamber of Deputies. Civil servant career / Chamber of Deputies The amendment to the Administrative Code regulates the career of civil servants and the management of contractual personnel. It concerns recruitment, competitions, promotion and performance evaluation. This reform is also linked to EUR 770 million from the PNRR. The stated goal is to build a system based on competencies and results. The project should clarify the career path of civil servants and the criteria used to fill management positions. Here too, there is no indication of a political conflict comparable to the disputes over salary or integrity. PSD has announced that it supports the project. The Senate was the first chamber to be notified, and the final vote belonged to the Chamber of Deputies. iulian@romania-insider.com (Photo source: Inquam Photos/George Calin) Read next 29 July 2026 Politics Romanian Parliament passes SAFE, PNRR-related bills during extraordinary session Normal Macro Four out of Romania’s six final RRF reform laws pass final vote in Parliament 31 July 2026 Iulian Ernst Like this article? Log in here » BUDAPEST, Hungary (AP) — Hungary’s foreign ministry has filed a criminal complaint with prosecutors over what it says was possible fraud related to the previous government’s purchase of ventilators worth some $965 million during the COVID-19 pandemic, Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said Tuesday. Hungary’s previous government under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán purchased the roughly 17,000 ventilators from China in March and April 2020, drawing criticism at the time that it was buying far more units than could be realistically deployed and paying much more per unit than other European countries. In a video posted to Facebook on Tuesday, Foreign Minister Orbán, who is not related to the former prime minister, said the results of a ministry investigation into the purchase “raises suspicions of breach of fiduciary duty causing particularly substantial financial loss and other criminal offenses.” FILE - Doctors and nurses wearing protective gears attend a patient on ventilator at the intensive care unit of Szent Laszlo Hospital treating COVID-19 patients during the pandemic of new coronavirus COVID-19 in Budapest, Hungary, on Dec. 13, 2021. (Zoltan Balogh/MTI via AP, File) She didn’t detail specific allegations, but noted that the investigation involved tens of thousands of documents — some of which had to be recovered using digital tools “after unsuccessful attempts to delete them” — and raised further questions “about the responsibility of the ministry’s former senior leadership.” A statement released on the Hungarian government’s website on Tuesday pointed to other suspected irregularities related to the ventilator procurement, including that most of the units were purchased through intermediary companies that saw their revenues rise exponentially due to the transaction. Some of the ventilators were defective, and a significant proportion of them was never deployed, the statement reads, adding that storage costs for the unused devices ran into the millions of dollars. Hungary’s former foreign minister Péter Szijjártó cultivated close ties with China during his nearly 12 years in office, and oversaw the purchase of the ventilators as well as the procurement of 5 million doses of the China-produced Sinopharm COVID-19 vaccine. Last month, Szijjártó resigned his seat in Parliament to take an executive position with Chinese automaker BYD, prompting accusations of a conflict of interest due to his role in facilitating substantial government subsidies given to the company while in office. Hungary’s government later launched an investigation into large investments into Hungary made by BYD during Szijjártó’s tenure. https://jowhar.com/polish-pm-defence-fac.text: Home NEWS WORLD NEWS ARTICLE POLITICS SPORT Somali TV Quran karim NEWS ARTICLE WORLD NEWS POLITICS Sport QURAN Video Somali TV privacy-policy terms and conditions Home NEWS WORLD NEWS ARTICLE POLITICS SPORT Somali TV Quran karim WORLD NEWS Facebook X Telegram WhatsApp ReddIt Pinterest Digg Donald Tusk said there was no doubt that the fire in Skarżysko-Kamienna was arson A pre-dawn blaze at a Polish defence manufacturer has been labelled “deliberate arson” by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, as authorities investigate a string of fires that has raised fresh concerns about sabotage. The fire broke out at a WB Group production plant in the south-central city of Skarżysko-Kamienna in the early hours of Monday morning. Local fire crews brought the flames under control after two hours, according to reports. WB Group makes components for drone systems, and its website says the group began producing reconnaissance drones in Ukraine last year. Polish police and the country’s Internal Security Agency are investigating the incident. The Skarżysko-Kamienna fire followed another major blaze last Sunday that damaged the warehouse of JFG Composites in the eastern city of Lublin. The company produces components for the aviation industry. “As far as the fires in two plants in Lublin and in Skarżysko-Kamienna are concerned, in the case of Skarżysko-Kamienna there is no doubt that there was deliberate arson, that is, an act of sabotage,” Mr Tusk told the media before a cabinet meeting in Warsaw this afternoon. He said investigators had not found the same kind of evidence pointing to arson in Lublin, but added “it cannot be ruled out taking into account the nature of the production”. Both factories were closed when the incidents occurred, and Polish authorities said no one was injured. Mr Tusk’s remarks come a day after the German government accused Russia of being behind an incident in August involving an explosive-laden drone at an airport in Leipzig. In response, the European Union and Ireland today summoned Russian ambassadors in Brussels and Dublin respectively to express concerns about the Leipzig incident. “There have been very disturbing incidents in the last few dozen hours in Poland, as well as in Germany,” said Mr Tusk. “This is a continuation of Russia’s escalation efforts throughout the region. Unfortunately, these are not the first cases and certainly, what is worse, not the last,” he said. Poland has accused Russian intelligence networks of orchestrating sabotage attacks on Polish soil since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine, including a fire at a shopping centre outside Warsaw in 2024 and an explosion which damaged a railway line in central-east Poland last November. Russia has denied any involvement in previous alleged sabotage incidents in Poland. https://www.huffingtonpost.co.uk/entry/n.text: What's Hot “I’m here to find an SS officer,” I told the uniformed guard outside the Berlin Archives. “He saved my mother,” I added in German. The guard handed me a visitor pass and a white plastic bag emblazoned with the German coat of arms – a black eagle with red talons – and directed me to a red brick building across a parade ground where thousands of SS officers once lined up. I registered inside. I explained to a librarian that I knew the officer was of Ukrainian background, but I did not know his name. I had already contacted archives in Poland, the U.S. and other parts of Germany in hopes of tracking down this man. Advertisement Most of what I knew about the SS officer came from my grandmother, who, for much of her life, kept what happened to her during World War II hidden. I first asked about the blue-green numbers on her arm when I was five, while watching her chop beets and onions for a soup. “It’s our phone number,” she said. “So I won’t forget it.” My grandmother continued to deflect my questions until she was in her 80s, when she finally let me interview her. But the gaps in her story alarmed me almost as much as her graphic descriptions, and after she died, I set out to fill them. To unravel her history. To understand how her experiences shaped her and my mother. To learn how a history I didn’t live ended up shaping me. Advertisement My grandmother first encountered the SS officer in a prison in Radom in Nazi-occupied Poland. The Polish Blue Police had arrested my grandparents at a factory my grandfather managed after they’d spent four years ducking and hiding from the Nazis using false names that hid their Jewish identities. One policeman ordered my grandmother to leave my mother behind. She picked up the screaming toddler, grabbed a white teddy bear, burrowed it into my mother’s cheek, and left her in her bed. Advertisement A policeman snapped cuffs on my grandparents’ wrists and led them outside. “Shoot us! Please shoot us!” My grandmother pleaded. She knew the Germans could kill her slowly as they attempted to learn how she’d obtained her fake papers. The policemen ignored her and bundled her and my grandfather into a car. Courtesy of Karen Kirsten The author's grandparents at their wedding in Warsaw, Poland, in 1938. Weeks later, on a frigid January morning, her prison cell door swung open, and my grandmother saw the SS officer: eyes set low below a bulbous forehead, stubby fingers taut as cigars. He locked shackles around her ankles, snapped cuffs on her wrists, and led her from the cell to interrogate her at Gestapo headquarters a mile away. Advertisement “He was a terrible fellow who was beating everyone,” my grandmother told me decades later. “A very famous, very cruel man, this fellow ... Ach! How he beat women! ” But she said, “he was like an angel with us.” This unsettled me. When she told me this, I knew nothing about the interrogation procedures at Gestapo headquarters or the torture tactics prisoners who survived later recounted, particularly those they suspected of having connections to the resistance, like my grandfather . Because of the floggings, starvation, slave labour and dehumanising treatment my grandmother endured in that prison and in Auschwitz and Ravensbrück, I doubt she was able to communicate the full picture of what they lived through. Maybe there was an even more horrific experience she needed to protect herself from reliving. Maybe the effects of whatever happened in that interrogation room were so devastating that she’d blocked the officer’s name from ever entering her mind again. She did not remember his name, but she would never forget him. Advertisement The plot to save my mother was my grandmother’s idea. Using sympathetic Polish guards as messengers, she smuggled coded suggestions to my grandfather’s cell on pieces of paper rolled to the size of a pea and stuffed into tiny cubes of bread. If her scheme did not go according to plan, she figured at the very least she would get to see my grandfather one last time before they shot her. Two months after their arrests, in the basement of Gestapo headquarters, a guard pushed my grandmother to the floor and locked her cuffs to an overhead pipe, next to my grandfather. Eventually, someone led them into a room more office-like than the interrogation cells. A light bulb hummed and flickered. The SS officer was already there. My grandfather sized up his boomerang eyebrows and his woolen uniform that, in the damp, smelled of horse. He scanned the room for whips, butcher hooks, and pokers. Advertisement Courtesy of Karen Kirsten "This photo of my mother was confiscated in Radom prison, returned and then smuggled through four concentration camps," the author writes. "It was taken in late 1943 before my grandparents were arrested." My grandmother sat by a desk beside my grandfather and rested her handcuffs on her thighs. She pulled awkwardly at her dress, which she’d been wearing since her arrest. She slid her fingers to the top of her stocking and fiddled and twisted. She unraveled the fabric wrapped around her upper leg and yanked hard. She pulled the corset off and kneaded slits in the fabric. Jewellery tumbled out. My grandmother had sewn her dead mother’s jewels into her clothing. Now she tilted the stones. They sparkled. She lowered gem-embellished earrings onto the desk. The diamonds in the rings were enormous. Advertisement Although my grandmother did not know the officer had taken bribes before, she hoped her mother’s jewels would seduce him. “What do you want?” he asked. “We want you to promise to save our child,” she told him. My grandmother had clung to the possibility that someone had heard my young mother screaming, but she did not know if the child was alive. She had no idea that someone had indeed found her and, at great risk, watched over this Jewish child. However, to this day, no one knows who. The SS officer drove 29 miles, found my mother, and delivered her to a convent. She remained hidden there for the rest of the war and was cared for by the nuns . Advertisement Courtesy of Karen Kirsten "This is my mother, Joasia, being held by Sister Stefania Sydry just after the SS officer delivered her to the convent in March 1944," the author writes. The officer’s superior ordered my grandparents to be sent to a nearby concentration camp instead of executing them. Later, they were forced – along with 3,300 others – to march 62 miles, and then they were loaded onto cattle cars bound for Auschwitz, where my grandmother was tattooed for slave labour. As the Soviets approached, the Germans transported my grandmother to Ravensbrück, where, from a sub-camp, she staggered, dizzy with hunger in -22 degrees Fahrenheit in her Auschwitz-issued wooden clogs with other “coat-hanger” women, as they called themselves, to an armaments factory to assemble bullets. Shortly before the war ended, Sweden’s Count Folk-Bernadotte made a deal with Heinrich Himmler, and the Red Cross evacuated my then 30-year-old grandmother. She arrived in Sweden on a stretcher. She weighed 59 pounds – unable to recall her name. My grandfather was sent from Auschwitz to Natzweiler, and then Dachau, where American soldiers eventually liberated him . Advertisement I was obsessed with finding the “good” Nazi who had taken my grandmother’s bribe. I could not stop thinking about how a man who embraced the ideology of exterminating people like my mother was also capable of choosing mercy. How he saved her. How without him, I would not exist. His one deed propagated my need to understand the choices victims and perpetrators make in violent times. It shaped everything from how I understand history to how I see the world I live in, to how I understand myself. Before visiting Berlin, I’d lurked in online forums, throwing names of officers at Radom prison at war buffs and collectors of Nazi memorabilia, trying to match details with what my grandmother had told me. I’d pestered every historian I could contact. I felt an irrational responsibility to thank the officer’s family. I wondered how a man who whipped and disfigured women – and pledged loyalty to a group that did so many unthinkable things – would treat his own children. I thought that if they knew about this kind act, it might help them bear a past they did not want as their legacy. A woman I met in Berlin connected me to an organisation that pairs descendants of Nazi perpetrators with survivors and their families – people on opposite sides of a shared history. One descendant combed German libraries and concentration camp archives for me. When I asked her why she was helping me, she told me she’d discovered later in life that her abusive father was a concentration camp commander. She said helping people broken by atrocities like the ones her father committed helped her grapple with a history she was born into. A history she did not choose. Advertisement After leaving Berlin without the officer’s name, I arrived at the U.S. Holocaust Museum in Washington, D.C., with low expectations. A researcher flipped through a file as thick as a book: prisoner ledgers, survivor lists, concentration camp inmate questionnaires, repatriation requests and denials. On the very last page of my grandfather’s file, I saw it: two SS lightning bolts typed in blue carbon ink, the Radom Gestapo unit that interrogated him, and a name. Shock arced through my stomach. It matched the name of a Ukrainian officer a historian had emailed me. It didn’t surprise me at all that my grandfather had stored the Nazi’s name in his head through four concentration camps and a death march and then revealed it to the Allies when they interviewed him. He had been a lawyer before the war, and at night from his bunk he’d urged fellow prisoners to recite SS officers’ names and their crimes so one day they could be tried. After his liberation , the U.S. military established the Dachau Trials and hired him to help prosecute high-ranking Nazis. However, after emigrating, like many refugees who reinvent themselves to match the expectations of new countries – and to suppress the horrors they escaped – he never talked about his past, much less the officer’s name. Courtesy of Karen Kirsten A photo of the author's grandfather when he was working with the U.S. Army at Dachau in 1946. Advertisement I found the SS officer’s family tree on a genealogy website. His daughter was about the same age as my 74-year-old mother. Maybe when the SS officer handed her to the Mother Superior at the convent , he was thinking about his own little girl he’d left behind. “He said, ‘Pray to God that the war will be finished and we can all go home soon,’” my grandmother told me. “Over and over, he said it.” I mailed a letter to his daughter: I hope this letter does not come as too much of a shock for you... Your father did something good for my family in 1944, particularly for my mother. I would not be alive and writing to you if it were not for him. Advertisement I omitted specifics. I intended to open a safe dialogue, but a week later the SS officer’s photo disappeared from the genealogy site. His tree was changed to “private” and blocked from my view. I never received a response. I thought I’d be able to establish for the officer’s daughter that whatever she knew about her father’s past, on one occasion he’d done something good. But perhaps I confronted her with questions she did not want to consider. I don’t know exactly what I thought I’d gain if I knew more, but part of me couldn’t rest until I did. It had nothing to do with forgiveness – not after what the Reich did to my family and millions of other families. I thought if I had reached her, she might have shared details about her father that humanised him. Made him less of a monster. But why would that make any difference? The fact is that he inflicted horrible atrocities on Polish prisoners. Maybe I hoped even the most heinous among us were capable of good. But how would knowing that in a tangible way change anything? I was left with the same question I’d started with: how can a murderer and saviour live in the same man? Advertisement My grandmother believed there is evil inside all of us. “When the opportunity comes up, like during the war... it happens,” she said. To this day, I don’t understand completely why she chose me as her confidante. Perhaps she knew I’d search for evidence to round out her unbearable memories, like a dog digging for a buried bone, unearthing horrible truths that were too traumatic for her to recall. I will never know the full extent of what that Nazi took from her. I read about officers who coerced women into sexual acts in exchange for food, to defer executions, to save a husband, a mother, a son, or a daughter. But this particular officer could have taken my grandmother’s jewels and killed her. By all accounts, that officer should have killed my mother, too. Whatever his motivations were, he saved their lives. Advertisement All my searching has taught me that truth, if we find it, can be ugly. The world isn’t straightforward – good or evil. Heroes can be repulsive, and the line between right or wrong, guilty or blameless, is not always clear. Despite this, whenever I find myself crediting the Nazi with decency, it feels like I’m betraying my grandmother. And the women he beat. And the millions of people the Nazis murdered. “You might forget the names,” my grandmother said. “But you don’t forget what happened.” The Holocaust didn’t start with gas chambers. It began when people decided a group of their fellow citizens was the enemy. My grandmother often said that when the societal norms of respect and decency collapse, we’re all capable of treating each other like animals. When we dehumanise others, we can find ways to justify the denial of rights and embrace all kinds of depravity and violence. The man whose name I found and chose not to make public for the sake of his daughter did unspeakable things. He is also the reason I exist. Advertisement Karen Kirsten is the author of Irena’s Gift, a 2025 National Jewish Book Award Finalist, winner of Zibby Awards for Best Family Drama & Best Story of Overcoming, and Australian Jewish Book Award Finalist. An Australian-American, Karen has lived in five countries and now calls the USA home. You can find more info about her at www.karenkirsten.com. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw5y.text: Image source, Federico Veronesi By Maddie Molloy & Alex Brian Climate & Science team Published 14 October 2026, 00:26 BST An emotional scene of an elephant carrying a deceased calf has earned Italian photographer Federico Veronesi the title of Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026. While tracking elephants in Namibia's Huab River Valley, Veronesi spotted an unusual trail of drag marks across the sand of a dry riverbed. Following the tracks, he came across a female elephant carrying a dead calf, its leg wedged between her tusk and trunk. Initially, Veronesi assumed the elephant was the calf's mother. But after sharing his photographs with an elephant research project working in the area, he learned that this wasn't certain. Researchers recognised the elephant as a female who had lost a calf several years earlier and said she had previously picked up dead calves belonging to other females. For Veronesi, the encounter was deeply significant. "Of all the 20 years I've done photographing animals, this is the most heart-wrecking and fascinating and dramatic," he said, describing it as "revealing of the depth and complexity of the emotions, the feelings of the animals." He hopes the image will encourage people to look beyond animals' physical appearance and recognise them as individuals with their own relationships, memories and emotions. "It's a small window that opens just a crack into the complexity of their world," he said. The competition's annual exhibition , external opens at the Natural History Museum on Friday 16 October 2026. Keep scrolling to see more award-winning images. Labour of love Image source, Oscar Whitfield Category : Young Grand Title and 11 to 14 Years Photographer : Oscar Whitfield, Zimbabwe/UK Location : Zambezi National Park, Zimbabwe Only by lying in the dust and capturing the beetle at eye level could Whitfield show how much strength its task required. While on a family game drive in Zimbabwe, near his home in Victoria Falls, he spotted the dung beetle struggling to push a ball of dung uphill through the sand, with a trail of flies following closely behind. After experimenting with different angles and compositions, he captured a moment that reveals the extraordinary effort involved in this seemingly simple task. "I hope that when people look at the photograph, they can see too, and maybe appreciate how much can be happening in a small moment in the natural world," says Whitfield. Flight of the Bumblebee Image source, Amelie Davis Category : 10 Years and Under Photographer : Amelie Davis, UK Location : Surrey, England You do not need a camera or a plane ticket to take an award-winning photo. Davis captured this shot in the garden using her dad's smartphone. The image freezes in time a single wingbeat from a common carder bumblebee as it prepares to land on a flower. The Meeting Place Image source, James Lewin Category : Animals in their Environment Photographer : James Lewin, UK Location : Chyulu Hills National Park, Kenya Lewin captured this dreamy, black-and-white photo of a young bull elephant spraying zebras at a waterhole. He softened the usually harsh light by using a camera converted to infrared. A Watchful Eye Image source, Aaron Sanders Category : Animal Portraits Photographer : Aaron Sanders, UK Location : Porthkerris Beach, Cornwall Common octopuses are usually found in the warmer Mediterranean Sea. But with global warming pushing up springtime sea temperatures, sightings across south-west England have massively increased. Sanders described the moment he spotted a single eye peeking from behind the kelp: "We remained perfectly still, watching one another with a seemingly shared curiosity." Scenes from the Swamp Image source, Isak Pretorius Category : Birds Photographer : Isak Pretorius, South Africa Location : Mabamba Swamp, Uganda Fewer than 5,300 mature shoebill storks are estimated to remain in the wild. Yet Pretorius, while canoeing with a guide, was able to capture these two â likely a breeding pair collecting material for their nest. Despite their name, shoebill storks are actually more closely related to pelicans, herons and ibises. Birdsong Painted in Light Image source, Konrad GrÃ¤eter Category : 15-17 Years Photographer : Konrad GrÃ¤eter, Germany Location : Baden-WÃ¼rttemberg, Germany Spring sees male blackbirds search for high vantage points to sing and try to attract a mate. This photo was taken in a vineyard at dawn, when the birds sing their most complex compositions. Urban Jungle Image source, Seth Forestson Category: Urban Wildlife Photographer: Seth Forestson, UK Location: Lumphini Park, Bangkok, Thailand Forestson lowered himself onto the mud to capture this common water lizard against the city skyline. These adaptable lizards live in cities across South and South East Asia and will take whatever food is available, such as catfish and koi. Making Morays Image source, Tony Wu Category: Under Water Photographer: Tony Wu, USA/Japan Location: Kagoshima Prefecture, KyÅ«shÅ«, Japan This is probably the first time the courtship ritual of Abbott's moray eels has been photographed, the NHM said. Wu worked with biologists and used dim red light and a customised fisheye lens to minimise disturbance. Wily Coyotes of San Francisco Image source, Loren Elliott Category: Photojournalist Story Award Photographer: Loren Elliott, USA Location: USA San Francisco is estimated to be home to around 100 coyotes, living alongside a large human population. While they can prey on domestic animals, they also help control disease-carrying rodents, and residents' attitudes towards them are mixed. Protective Pose Image source, Anton Sorokin Category: Behaviour: Amphibians and Reptiles Photographer: Anton Sorokin, US Location: Contra Costa County, California, USA Sorokin dipped his camera and lights in a murky pond to catch this glimpse of a California newt laying her eggs. Shifting Sand Image source, Sitaram Raul Category : Behaviour: Invertebrates Photographer: Sitaram Raul, India Location: Thar Desert, Rajasthan, India A scorpion is photographed burrowing into the shifting dunes of India's Thar Desert. Exploring the dunes at night, Raul saw many scorpions searching for prey but as temperatures rose after sunrise, the scorpion dug into the sand to escape the intense heat. Night-Time Catch Image source, Alex Lindbloom, USA Category: Oceans: The Bigger Picture Photographer: Alex Lindbloom, USA Location: Off Cenderawasih Bay, Papua, Indonesia A whale shark investigates the catch of a mobile net-fishing platform, known as a bagan. Lindbloom searched for sharks around dawn, using the bagan's bright lights to illuminate them when there was too little natural light for his drone. Shedding Light Image source, Agorastos Papatsanis Category: Plants and Fungi Photographer: Agorastos Papatsanis, Greece Location: Litochoro, Pieria, Greece Papatsanis used ultrviolet light to illuminate mushrooms known as "beautiful bonnets" growing from a decaying log on the lower slopes of Mount Olympus in Greece. Hidden Depths Image source, Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas Category: Rising Star Award Photographer: Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas, Germany Location: Germany and Northern Ireland, UK Tinker-Tsavalas uses macro photography to reveal the intricate details of tiny animals that are easily overlooked, particularly in urban habitats. His interest in macro photography developed during the Covid-19 lockdowns, when he was restricted to habitats close to his home in Berlin. Escape Artistry Image source, MichaÅ Michalski Category: Natural Artistry Photographer: MichaÅ Michalski, Poland Location: Litochoro, Pieria, Greece Michalski used a slow shutter speed to photograph birds flying across a background of leafless birch trees. A field of unharvested sunflowers had attracted mixed flocks of birds, especially goldfinches and bramblings, before they were startled into the air by a sparrowhawk. The Great Divide Image source, Alex Visbal Category: Wetlands: The Bigger Picture Photographer: Alex Visbal, Colombia Location: Stansbury Bay, Great Salt Lake, Utah, USA Visbal documents how a single engineered line can reshape an entire wetland as part of a long-term project on the industrial impact on waterways. The pink comes from microbes thriving in extremely salty water after the area was cut off from fresh water. Warning Sign Image source, Francisco Negroni Category: Photojournalism Photographer: Francisco Negroni, Chile Location: Route 40, Santa Cruz Province, Argentina Negroni records this scene of a dead puma displayed as a hunting trophy in Santa Cruz, a province in Argentine Patagonia. Although Santa Cruz banned puma hunting in 2025, illegal persecution continues. Secret Worlds Image source, Kutub Uddin Category: Portfolio Award Photographer: Kutub Uddin, Bangladesh/UK Location: West Sussex, England, UK Uddin's photographs explore the miniature world of slime moulds, organisms that can be barely visible to the naked eye and whose fruiting structures are just one to two millimetres high.
